clue.text: Categorise form of questionable quality half-heartedly

parts.note: a form is a school class, a year group of pupils

indicators.note: half the heart taken away: one of the two central letters is dropped from the word

parts.note: something of questionable quality is iffy, dubious

explanation.surface: A teacher grudgingly sorts a dubious piece of paperwork into its category.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-heartedly' removes one F from the middle of IFFY, leaving IFY.
explanation.definitionFit: To classify things is to sort them into categories, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Cleaner has a child showing great charm

parts.note: a char, or charwoman, is a cleaning lady in British usage
a woman who has a child is a ma, so the phrase reads as IS MA

explanation.surface: A cleaning lady with a baby wins everyone over with her personality.
explanation.walkthrough: CHAR is British for a cleaning woman; 'has a child' is read playfully as 'is (a) ma', giving IS MA.
explanation.definitionFit: Charisma is a compelling personal magnetism, the power of great charm over others.

clue.text: Suitable party's introduced to choose as candidate

indicators.note: the short form of 'is' plus 'introduced to' says one word is put into the other

parts.note: apt means suitable or fitting
a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: A fitting political party gets brought in to select its election candidate.
explanation.definitionFit: A party adopts a candidate when it formally selects that person to stand for it.

clue.text: One-sided argument of constable over what policeman has?

indicators.note: in a down entry one piece placed over another comes first

parts.note: a special constable, or special, is a volunteer part-time police officer
the word policeman has P leading it, as its first letter, so the phrase reads P LEADING

explanation.surface: A constable presents a biased case about what officers are owed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' puts SPECIAL above the second piece in this down entry; the question mark flags that 'what policeman has' is read literally: the letter P leading.
explanation.definitionFit: Special pleading is argument that cites only the points favourable to one's own side, a set legal and debating term.

clue.text: One needs to change if such a colour

indicators.note: the letters of the words beside it need changing into a new order

parts.note: one is A, as in a single thing

explanation.surface: Someone is told to alter their outfit if it is such a garish shade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to change' rearranges IF SUCH into FUCHSI; A for 'One' follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: Fuchsia is a vivid purplish-pink shade, named after the flowering shrub.

clue.text: Man perhaps exists to catch fish

parts.note: is means exists, as in 'there is'
to land a fish is to catch it and bring it ashore

explanation.surface: Somebody survives by fishing for a living.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is the Isle of Man in the Irish Sea, not a person; 'perhaps' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man is an example of an island, signalled by 'perhaps'.

clue.text: What might shift under LA, SF and Santa A?

definitions.text: What might shift under LA, SF and Santa A?

indicators.note: shifting moves the letters of the following words into a new order

parts.note: Los Angeles, written as its abbreviation
San Francisco, written as its abbreviation
Santa Ana, a Californian city, shortened

explanation.surface: A question about what geological movement lies beneath California's big cities.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of UNDER, LA, SF and SANTA A, leaving out the joining 'and', are shuffled ('might shift') into the answer, which is also what the whole clue describes.
explanation.definitionFit: The San Andreas Fault is the Californian fault line whose movement causes earthquakes under those cities.

clue.text: Incredulity as a labyrinth's designed for the ear

indicators.note: the phrase is to be spoken, giving a word with the same sound

parts.note: a labyrinth is a maze and designed is meant, so the phrase reads A MAZE MEANT

explanation.surface: Astonishment that a maze was laid out purely for listening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for the ear' says A MAZE MEANT, said aloud, gives the answer's sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Amazement is astonished disbelief, close in sense to incredulity.

clue.text: Engine stops working on elevated railway

parts.note: a machine that dies stops working
the El is the American name for an elevated railway, as in Chicago

explanation.surface: A locomotive breaks down on an overhead track.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'on' puts DIES above EL.
explanation.definitionFit: A diesel is an engine, or a locomotive, driven by compression-ignited oil fuel.

clue.text: Courageous and fortunate under pressure

indicators.note: in a down entry the piece under another comes below it

parts.note: P is the physics symbol for pressure
lucky means fortunate

explanation.surface: Someone shows bravery and good luck when the pressure is on.
explanation.definitionFit: Plucky describes someone showing pluck, spirited courage in difficulty.

clue.text: Greatly love an artist known for his illustrations

parts.note: Gustave Doré was the French artist famous for illustrating the Bible, Dante and other books

explanation.surface: Someone is devoted to a famous illustrator's work.
explanation.definitionFit: To adore is to love deeply, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Doone clan involved supporters in a row

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so these letters are mixed together

explanation.surface: The Doone family from Lorna Doone are lined up like pillars in the story.
explanation.walkthrough: The Doones are the outlaw clan of Blackmore's novel Lorna Doone; 'involved' scrambles DOONE CLAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A colonnade is a row of columns, which support a roof or entablature.

clue.text: Carpet laid out for empress

parts.note: a mat is a small carpet or rug

indicators.note: out means disordered, so the letters of the neighbouring word are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rug is spread out for a visiting royal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges LAID into ILDA. Matilda was the 12th-century English claimant who was also Holy Roman Empress.
explanation.definitionFit: The Empress Matilda, daughter of Henry I, was wife of the Holy Roman Emperor Henry V.

clue.text: Went with a pony to roam common

indicators.note: roaming wanders about, so the letters stray into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone set off with a pony to ride across the village green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to roam' shuffles WENT and A PONY; 'with' only joins. 'Common' is the adjective, not the village green it suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Two-a-penny is a British idiom for something so plentiful it is cheap and ordinary.

clue.text: Perhaps member of Yankees doesn't want fresh ball

indicators.note: not wanting something means it is left out of the longer word

parts.note: a New York Yankees player might be a New Yorker
fresh means new

explanation.surface: A baseball player turns down a new ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doesn't want' drops NEW from NEW YORKER. A yorker is a cricket delivery pitched right at the batsman's feet, not a baseball term.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a yorker is a ball bowled to land at or just under the batsman's bat.

clue.text: Dickens' hero involved in dull and menial work

indicators.note: one piece is wrapped inside the other

parts.note: dry means dull and uninteresting
Barnaby Rudge is the title hero of a Dickens novel

explanation.surface: A Dickens character is caught up in boring, lowly labour.
explanation.definitionFit: Drudgery is hard, tedious and menial work.

clue.text: Sauce heard from Eastern labourer

indicators.note: what is heard is a word of the same sound

parts.note: a coolie was an unskilled labourer in India or China, now an offensive term

explanation.surface: Someone learns a sauce recipe from a worker in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heard from' gives a word sounding like COOLIE.
explanation.definitionFit: A coulis is a thin puree of fruit or vegetables served as a sauce.

clue.text: Hill in south-east with unknown level of building

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: SE is the compass abbreviation for south-east
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor
y is a mathematical unknown

explanation.surface: A hill in south-east England hides an unexplained floor of some building.
explanation.definitionFit: A storey is one floor or level of a building.

clue.text: Shilling gets milliner greatly upset

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for the old British shilling coin
a hatter, like a milliner, makes hats

explanation.surface: A hatmaker is very distressed at being paid a mere shilling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'greatly upset' has two words but is all definition; 'gets' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: To shatter someone is to distress them severely, a figurative sense of breaking to pieces.

clue.text: One day I dined and got to fill up

parts.note: Sat is short for Saturday, one day of the week
ate means dined

explanation.surface: On one particular day the speaker had a meal and became full.
explanation.definitionFit: To satiate is to satisfy fully, to fill someone up with food.

clue.text: A pointer to earth growing cold

definitions.text: A pointer to earth growing cold

parts.words: A pointer to earth growing cold
parts.note: a frozen spike hanging from a roof points down to the ground and lengthens as the weather turns colder

explanation.surface: A compass needle or signpost gets chillier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pointer' suggests a dog or a needle; here it is something that points down, and 'growing' is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: An icicle is a hanging tapering spike of ice, pointing downward and forming in freezing weather.

clue.text: What gives oil company public relations answer

explanation.surface: An oil firm's press office supplies an answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Copra is dried coconut kernel, from which coconut oil is pressed.

clue.text: How card may be played without consideration

definitions.meaning: a card is played from the hand, held by the player
dismissed at once, without being thought about

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is literal card-playing; the second is the idiom for rejecting something immediately.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase literally describes a card taken from one's hand, and idiomatically means summarily, without thought.

clue.text: Silver appearing above eroded stone

indicators.note: in a down entry this piece stands on top of the next

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
ate means wore away, eroded

explanation.surface: Silver shows up over a worn-away rock.
explanation.definitionFit: Agate is a banded semi-precious stone, a variety of chalcedony.

clue.text: Melody lies oddly in a bar

indicators.note: one piece is put inside the other

parts.note: a cantina is a bar, especially in Spanish-speaking countries

indicators.note: taking the odd-numbered letters picks the first and third of the word

explanation.surface: A tune is played badly in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' takes L and E from 'lies'; 'in' puts them inside CANTINA.
explanation.definitionFit: A cantilena is a smooth, lyrical vocal melody, a musical term.

clue.text: Undersecretary's mature practice

parts.note: US is the abbreviation for undersecretary
to age is to mature

explanation.surface: A junior minister has a well-established routine.
explanation.definitionFit: Usage means customary practice, the habitual way something is done.

clue.text: Sea holly tangled up in groyne

indicators.note: tangling means the letters of the next word get mixed up

explanation.surface: A coastal plant is caught in a sea defence on the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: A groyne is a low wall built out into the sea to stop beach erosion; 'tangled up' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: Eryngo is the plant genus Eryngium, whose best-known member is sea holly.

clue.text: Some will eat her Yorkshire that's rather tough

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A diner warns that some Yorkshire pudding will prove chewy.
explanation.definitionFit: Leathery describes food that is tough and chewy like leather.
